title: Christmas: the Word again (John 1:14)
hook: at Christmas, churches read John's prologue: the Word became flesh
tomorrow: Year two close: the book in your hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, how to keep reading, and your line was the book keeps opening. Which book did you choose, and what caught you? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Two Christmas readings, and they could hardly be more different. One is from Luke: shepherds, a manger, angels over the fields at night. The other is from John, and it has no manger at all. No shepherds, no star, no inn. It starts before time: in the beginning was the Word. In many churches, Luke's story is read at night, and John's opening is read on Christmas morning, or as the last reading at a candlelit service of lessons and carols. You read both Gospels this year. Today we come back to one verse in John, the one that makes it a Christmas text.

John's Gospel opens the way Genesis does. In the King James Bible: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word, in Greek the logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind everything. Then: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." And then the verse the whole passage leans toward, verse fourteen: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." You met this verse in the autumn, through its tent: dwelt, in Greek, is pitched his tent. At Christmas, churches lean on the other word. Flesh. In Greek, sarx, the plain word for the stuff of bodies. John could have said the Word appeared, or visited. He says it became flesh. Not an idea, not a voice from the sky. At Christmas that flesh is a baby: someone who has to be fed, changed, carried and kept warm. Christians say the Word that was there in the beginning started out that small. Churches keep the day a little differently. Many celebrate on December twenty-fifth; many Orthodox churches that follow the older Julian calendar celebrate on what is now January seventh. Catholic, Anglican and many Protestant churches read this prologue on Christmas Day. In the Orthodox liturgy for the Nativity, the Gospel is Matthew's story of the Magi, and John's prologue is read at Easter instead. Same verse, same wonder, different places in the year. Luke tells you where he was born. John tells you who was born.
screen: `A BABY WHO HAS TO BE FED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read John 1:1–14 by a light. If you can, turn the room lights down and light one lamp or candle, safely. Settle, and breathe. Open to the first chapter of John and read the first fourteen verses slowly, out loud if you like. When you reach the light shining in the darkness, look at the flame for one breath. When you reach the Word made flesh, think of one ordinary body you love: a hand, a face, a child asleep. Christians say God came that close. If you pray, you can read verse fourteen once more, slowly, as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Christmas. The feast of the birth of Jesus, when John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and pitched his tent among us.
Your line: he dwelt among us. Today, look for the holy in something ordinary and close by: a meal, a voice, a face across the table. Day six hundred ninety-five.

fork.setup: you're John, writing the story of Jesus. the other Gospels tell of his birth and family. where do you begin?
options: with a list of his ancestors.
fork.reveal: "In the beginning was the Word." John starts before creation, echoing Genesis, and only then: the Word was made flesh.

original.note: Greek: became flesh, in John 1:14. sarx is the plain word for flesh, the stuff of bodies.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christmas is only the manger story.
what it means: John tells Christmas without a manger: the Word that was there in the beginning became flesh.
what a scholar hears: sarx egeneto, became flesh, the plainest word for a body; and Orthodox churches read this prologue at Easter, not at the Nativity.

notes: Liturgical claims: John 1:1–14 (or 1–18) as the Christmas Day Gospel in Catholic and Anglican use and as the ninth lesson at lessons and carols; Orthodox Nativity Gospel Matthew 2:1–12 and John 1:1–17 at Pascha. Confirm.
Julian-calendar Christmas falls on January 7 in the civil calendar (currently); framed as 'what is now January seventh'.
ἐσκήνωσεν from σκηνόω / σκηνή; the Septuagint uses σκηνή for the tabernacle. Confirm.
'Incarnation, from the Latin for being made flesh' (incarnatio). Confirm phrasing.
Softened in review: the tabernacle echo in eskenosen framed as how many readers hear John, not as settled; hook's 'no innkeeper' changed to 'no inn', since Luke 2:7 names an inn but no innkeeper.
